_comment: Hand-written question bank for local quiz testing (seed_quiz.py). Covers only the kubernetes topic's beginner tier -- enough to run a full quiz end to end against seeded data. Not the real generator output (task 0012).

questions.card_title: A kubectl apply doesn't talk to the scheduler directly
questions.stem: When you run `kubectl apply`, what does the client actually talk to?
options: The scheduler directly
The API server
Whichever node has capacity
etcd directly
questions.explanation: Every actor in the system, including the scheduler itself, only ever talks to the API server, which is backed by etcd.

questions.card_title: A pod is the unit of scheduling
questions.stem: What is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules onto a node?
options: A container
A pod
A deployment
A namespace
questions.explanation: Kubernetes never schedules a container directly -- it schedules a pod, which may hold one or more containers that always land together.

questions.card_title: The scheduler filters, then scores
questions.stem: What happens if the scheduler's filtering phase removes every node as a candidate?
options: The pod is scheduled onto a random node anyway
The pod stays Pending
The pod crashes with CrashLoopBackOff
The API server retries filtering with looser constraints
questions.explanation: If filtering removes every node, the pod stays Pending -- that is the failure you actually see, before scoring ever runs.

questions.card_title: Requests are for the scheduler, limits are for the kernel
questions.stem: What's the practical consequence of exceeding a container's memory limit, versus its CPU limit?
options: Both get throttled the same way
Exceeding CPU gets you OOM-killed; memory just throttles
Exceeding memory gets you OOM-killed; CPU just throttles
Neither is enforced by the kernel
questions.explanation: Exceeding a CPU limit gets you throttled (slow, but alive); exceeding a memory limit gets you OOM-killed.

questions.card_title: Pending is a scheduling problem, CrashLoopBackOff is yours
questions.stem: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. Where's the problem?
options: The scheduler couldn't place it
Placement worked; something in your container is failing after it starts
The node ran out of IP addresses
The API server is unreachable
questions.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff means placement worked fine -- the problem is inside your container, not the scheduler.

questions.card_title: Labels are the only way things find each other
questions.stem: How does a Service know which pods belong to it?
options: It holds a static list of pod IPs
It holds a label selector, recomputed continuously
Pods register themselves with the Service on startup
It reads a pointer stored in etcd
questions.explanation: A Service holds a label selector, not a list of pods -- membership is recomputed continuously, which is also why a label typo breaks routing silently.

questions.card_title: The scheduler filters, then scores
questions.stem: Explain the two phases the Kubernetes scheduler uses to place a pod, and why only one of them can cause the pod to stay Pending.
questions.rubric: 0: no mention of two phases. 1: names filtering and/or scoring but doesn't explain the failure mode. 2: correctly explains filtering removes ineligible nodes and scoring ranks the rest. 3: level 2 plus a correct, specific reason only filtering can leave the pod Pending (scoring only ranks nodes that already passed filtering, so it can't reduce the candidate set to zero).
questions.reference_answer: Placing a pod happens in two phases. Filtering removes nodes that cannot run the pod at all -- insufficient CPU or memory, an intolerable taint, an unsatisfiable node selector. Scoring then ranks whatever nodes are left. If filtering removes every node, the pod stays Pending; scoring never gets a chance to run because there is nothing left to score.

questions.card_title: A Service is a stable name for an unstable set
questions.stem: Why does Kubernetes need a Service in front of a set of pods, rather than callers just addressing pod IPs directly?
options: Pod IPs are ephemeral and change when a pod restarts
Pods don't have IP addresses at all
Direct pod-to-pod traffic is disabled by default
Services are required for DNS to work at all
questions.explanation: Pod IPs are ephemeral -- a pod restarts and gets a new one. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a continuously re-evaluated set of pods.

questions.card_title: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer are layers, not alternatives
questions.stem: How do the three common Service types relate to each other?
options: They are three independent, mutually exclusive choices
NodePort is a ClusterIP plus a port opened on every node; LoadBalancer adds a cloud load balancer on top
LoadBalancer is the base type that the others restrict
ClusterIP only works outside the cluster
questions.explanation: The three types stack: ClusterIP is the base, NodePort is a ClusterIP plus a node-level port, and LoadBalancer is a NodePort plus a cloud load balancer.

questions.card_title: kube-proxy does not proxy much any more
questions.stem: In its usual iptables/IPVS mode, what does kube-proxy actually do to Service traffic?
options: It sits in the data path as a userspace proxy for every request
It programs kernel rules that rewrite Service IP traffic to a pod IP, then steps aside
It forwards every packet through a Go process
It does nothing -- the name is entirely vestigial
questions.explanation: Despite the name, kube-proxy mostly doesn't sit in the data path -- it programs kernel rules once, and the kernel handles traffic from then on.

questions.card_title: A Service is a stable name for an unstable set
questions.stem: A teammate says "I'll just hardcode this pod's IP in our config, it's simpler." Explain what will break, and why a Service avoids the problem.
questions.rubric: 0: no understanding of the problem. 1: vague mention that IPs change, without connecting it to a concrete failure. 2: correctly explains pod IPs are ephemeral and hardcoding breaks on restart/rescheduling. 3: level 2 plus explains how a Service's label-selector-based, continuously re-evaluated membership fixes it (stable virtual IP/DNS name in front of a changing pod set).
questions.reference_answer: Pod IPs are ephemeral: the moment that pod restarts or gets rescheduled, it gets a new IP, and the hardcoded config now points at nothing. A Service avoids this by giving callers a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a set of pods that is continuously re-evaluated from a label selector, so the caller never needs to learn or track individual pod IPs.

questions.card_title: Everything is a reconciliation loop
questions.stem: You delete a pod that's owned by a Deployment. What happens, and why?
options: Nothing comes back -- deleting a pod removes it from the desired state too
A new pod comes back, because you deleted an observation, not the underlying intention
The Deployment itself is deleted along with it
It comes back only if you also restart the controller manager
questions.explanation: Kubernetes controllers declare desired state, not commands. Deleting a pod removes an observation, not the intention that three should exist, so the controller replaces it.

questions.card_title: Everything is a reconciliation loop
questions.stem: What does a Kubernetes controller fundamentally do, on a loop?
options: Executes a queue of commands in order
Compares desired state to observed state and acts to close the gap
Waits for an admin to approve each change
Replays the cluster's event log from the beginning
questions.explanation: A controller repeatedly compares desired state to observed state and acts to close the gap -- it is not a command executor.

questions.card_title: Level-triggered, not edge-triggered
questions.stem: Why is Kubernetes robust against a controller missing a single notification?
options: Notifications are delivered over a guaranteed-once channel
Controllers act on current state, not on events, so the next resync fixes any missed discrepancy anyway
Missed notifications are automatically retried by etcd
Every controller keeps its own persistent event log
questions.explanation: Controllers are level-triggered: they act on current state, not on individual events, so a missed notification is caught by the next resync instead of being lost.

questions.card_title: Level-triggered, not edge-triggered
questions.stem: What would an edge-triggered design require that a distributed system can't promise?
options: That every node has the same clock
That every event arrives exactly once
That the API server never restarts
That etcd is single-node
questions.explanation: An edge-triggered design would need every event to arrive exactly once -- not something a distributed system can promise -- which is why controllers are level-triggered instead.

questions.card_title: Deployments do not manage pods
questions.stem: What sits between a Deployment and the pods it's ultimately responsible for?
options: Nothing -- a Deployment manages pods directly
A ReplicaSet
A DaemonSet
A ConfigMap
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and a ReplicaSet manages pods -- that middle layer is what makes rollbacks work.

questions.card_title: Deployments do not manage pods
questions.stem: Why does the ReplicaSet layer make a Deployment rollback simple?
options: Each revision gets its own ReplicaSet, so rolling back is just scaling the old one back up
Rollbacks reconstruct the previous spec from Kubernetes' audit log
ReplicaSets store no state, so there is nothing to roll back
Rollbacks always require deleting and recreating the Deployment
questions.explanation: Each Deployment revision gets its own ReplicaSet. A rollback just scales the old ReplicaSet back up -- its spec still exists, so nothing needs to be reconstructed.

questions.card_title: Deployments do not manage pods
questions.stem: What is the intermediate object between a Deployment and its pods?
options: ReplicaSet
StatefulSet
Ingress
PersistentVolumeClaim
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and a ReplicaSet manages the pods -- that intermediate object is what makes rollback simple.

questions.card_title: Readiness and liveness answer different questions
questions.stem: A pod fails its readiness probe. What happens?
options: The container is killed and restarted
The pod is removed from Service endpoints; nothing is killed
The whole Deployment is rolled back
The node is cordoned
questions.explanation: Readiness controls traffic, not restarts: failing it just removes the pod from Service endpoints.

questions.card_title: Readiness and liveness answer different questions
questions.stem: What's the risk of using a liveness probe where you actually meant readiness?
options: There is no risk, they're interchangeable
A slow startup or brief dependency outage turns into a restart loop, potentially cascading under load
The pod would simply never restart
It would silently disable health checking entirely
questions.explanation: Liveness controls restarts. Using it for what should be a readiness check turns a transient slow-start or dependency blip into a restart loop -- and under load, that can cascade as every restart makes the remaining pods busier.

questions.card_title: Everything is a reconciliation loop
questions.stem: Explain what "level-triggered, not edge-triggered" means for how Kubernetes controllers behave, and why that design choice matters for a distributed system.
questions.rubric: 0: no understanding. 1: repeats the terms without explaining the mechanism. 2: correctly explains controllers act on current observed state rather than individual events. 3: level 2 plus explains why this matters -- a missed event is self-healing on the next resync, whereas an edge-triggered design would require exactly-once event delivery, which a distributed system cannot guarantee.
questions.reference_answer: Level-triggered means a controller acts on current state -- what is actually true right now -- rather than reacting to individual events. It repeatedly compares desired state to observed state and closes the gap. This matters because it makes the system robust to missed messages: if a controller misses a notification, the next resync still sees the same discrepancy and fixes it. An edge-triggered design would instead require every event to arrive exactly once, which no distributed system can promise.
